identification.bodyShape: Standard Sebastes fusiform, moderately compressed rockfish body. Interorbital space (between the eyes) is convex, and head spines are typically absent.
identificationTraits: Three pores on each side of the lower jaw and two dark bars on each cheek (ADF&G field key).
Convex space between the eyes; head spines typically absent (NOAA/AFSC rockfish field guide).
Fin ray counts: dorsal XIII,13-16; anal 7-9; pectoral 17-19; gill rakers 32-36 (NOAA/AFSC rockfish field guide).
Peritoneum (body-cavity lining) light to dark, versus dark rockfish's uniformly dark peritoneum.
identification.coloration: Gray to greenish-brown on the back and sides, with darker blotches beneath the soft dorsal fin. Ventral side and the pectoral and pelvic fins are tinged pink; sides show orange-red-brown flecks; belly pale pink to whitish.
identification.adultAppearance: A brownish-gray to greenish-brown rockfish with pink-tinged fins and belly, orange-red flecking on the sides, and the diagnostic jaw pores and cheek bars. Reaches roughly 21-23 in (53-59 cm).

similarSpecies.name: Dark rockfish (Sebastes ciliatus)
similarSpecies.distinction: Dark rockfish is uniformly black to dark blue on the back and sides with a uniformly dark peritoneum, versus dusky rockfish's brownish-gray to greenish-brown cast, pink-tinged fins and belly, and light-to-dark peritoneum. The two were treated as a single species until Orr & Blackburn (2004) resurrected S. variabilis as distinct from a redescribed S. ciliatus; they remain easy to confuse in the field.

similarSpecies.name: Widow rockfish / yellowtail rockfish / black rockfish (other Alaska pelagic-shelf rockfish)
similarSpecies.distinction: ADF&G's rockfish identification guide separates dusky from these look-alikes using the jaw pores and cheek bars (absent or different on the others) together with dusky's pink/orange fin and belly tint, versus widow rockfish's more uniform brown/brass cast and yellowtail rockfish's distinctly yellowish fins.

identification.averageAdultLength: Not found as a distinct 'average' figure in sourced material; see maximumDocumentedSize.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Reported maximum length varies slightly by source: the NOAA/AFSC rockfish field guide gives 21 in (56 cm), while ADF&G/stock-assessment materials give up to 23.2 in (59 cm). Both are recorded here rather than picking one.
identification.longevity: Long-lived: oldest recorded fishery sample was 76 years old (NPFMC/AFSC Gulf of Alaska stock assessment); age at 50% maturity is about 10.3 years, at roughly 40.6 cm.

social.note: ADF&G's own regulatory identification guidance classifies dusky rockfish as a "pelagic rockfish" -- an open-water species found mid-water in schools near rocky structure, rather than a solitary bottom-hugger.

feedingStrategy.note: Adult diet is dominated by euphausiids (krill) and Pacific sand lance, together accounting for about 99% of stomach contents in recent Gulf of Alaska sampling -- consistent with mid-water plankton/small-fish feeding rather than benthic feeding (NPFMC/AFSC stock assessment).

dielTendency.note: No species-specific diel activity data (day vs. night feeding timing) were found in sourced material. "Mixed" is recorded here as an honest placeholder, not a sourced finding -- see gaps.

behavior.depthMovement: Adults hold at roughly 100-200 m on offshore banks and shelf gullies; older juveniles occupy shallower, more inshore water than adults, per the Gulf of Alaska stock assessment. No finer-grained seasonal depth shift is documented.
behavior.coverUse: Associates with rocky substrate, sponge beds, and coral on offshore banks and shelf gullies (NPFMC/AFSC stock assessment).
behavior.spawningBehavior: Ovoviviparous (live-bearing); parturition of larvae is believed to occur in spring, based on ripe females sampled on an April Gulf of Alaska research cruise. As in other Sebastes, mating and fertilization occur separately from the spring release of larvae; the timing of mating is not documented in sourced material. No spawning location or aggregation is named.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Dusky rockfish biology is best documented around its spring parturition timing and its year-round association with offshore banks and shelf gullies at 100-200 m. Sourced material does not describe a season-by-season habitat shift beyond that, so most seasons are represented here only by the general habitat description with an explicit note that no distinct seasonal shift is documented.

entries.habitatClass: Offshore banks and outer continental shelf gullies at roughly 100-200 m over rocky substrate, sponge beds, and coral -- the general adult habitat.
entries.conservationNote: Live-bearing rockfish; larval release (parturition) is believed to occur in spring based on ripe females sampled on an April Gulf of Alaska research cruise. No spawning concentration or location is described or implied.
entries.presentationImplication: Deep-drop and vertical-jig presentations that reach the 100-200 m band remain the reviewed approach for this depth; this is a habitat/depth note, not a seasonal bite claim.
invalidators: treating spring parturition timing as a feeding or catch cue
